messages.subject: Export ROI as Data Frame
messages.body_plain:
Dear Cardinal MSI Help & Kylie Bemis

I wish to inquire if its possible to select multiple region of interest and write/export/save them as data frames (with all the mass features and intensities) for further multivariate analysis.
Here is my code below.

ROI_5 <-  selectROI(data1_processed, formula = ~ x * y,

Select pixels and press ESC or second mouse button when done

messages.subject: Re: Export ROI as Data Frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shadrack,

Firstly, I'll note you don't really need most of those arguments to selectROI() besides the first one (and possibly "main"), as they're all the defaults anyway.

As for selecting multiple ROI, it depends what do you want to do with them? The ROI are simply returned as a logical vector, so you can manipulate them as you wish.

For example, if you selected two ROI and assigned them to variables "roi1" and "roi2", you could do:

myroi <- roi1 | roi2

to combine them into a single larger ROI using R's vectorized "OR" operator.

You could also do:

condition <-rep(NA_character_, ncol(mydata)
condition[roi1] <- "Condition 1"
condition[roi2] <- "Condition 2"
condition <- as.factor(condition)

to create a categorical variable (a factor) with two ROI's in it.

How do you want the data frame of intensities and masses formatted? Do you want, for example, each column to be a mass spectrum?

You could do this like:

myroi <- selectROI(mydata)
myroi_spectra <- as.data.frame(spectra(mydata)[,myroi])
write.csv(myroi_spectra, file="spectra.csv")
write.csv(pData(mydata)[myroi,], file="coord.csv")
write.csv(fData(mydata), file="mz.csv")

In this case, each column of "spectra.csv" is a mass spectrum, and the pixel coordinates and m/z values are stored in separate CSV files.

Does this accomplish what you want?

-Kylie

messages.subject: Normalization pending
messages.body_plain:
Yes, for “MSImagingExperiment” objects, preprocessing methods are not applied immediately but are queued to the object. This is so that you can queue multiple processing steps and apply them all at once, which can be more efficient if the data is very large.

Simply call “process(data)” on the object to apply any queued preprocessing steps.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Normalization pending
messages.body_plain:
Yes. Part of the idea is also that you can chain preprocessing steps in a way that is conceptually expressive using the piping operator "%>%":

data_preproc <- data %>%
    normalize() %>%
    peakPick() %>%
    peakAlign() %>%
    select(x==1, y==1) %>%
    process(plot=TRUE)

Note that the "plot" options for preprocessing steps are now in the process() method as well, along with options for parallelization using the BPPARAM argument (see "BiocParallel" package for details).

In the example above, you can queue several preprocessing steps, and then use select() to subset to a few pixels to a preview, and apply the processing on those pixels using process().

(The piping operator is borrowed from the "magrittr" package and is widely used in some parts of the R world such as the "tidyverse" packages like "dplyr".)

The "Cardinal 2.0 User's Guide" vignette has a limited description of this that will be expanded in the next release.

("MSImageSet" remains the default import setting for now, but this will change in the next release when more infrastructure for "MSImagingExperiment" is in place. All previous functionality will be retained for backward-compatibility purposes.)

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: BiocParallel errors while normalizing
messages.body_plain:
You have a couple options. Your spectra are currently an on-disk 'matter' matrix, so they are not loaded into memory.

The default for on-disk data is to treat it as read-only, which is why your first version has an error.

If the dataset is small enough to load into memory, then you can simply do:

spectra(data[[3]]) <- as.matrix(spectra(data[[3]]))
spectra(data[[3]])[is.na(spectra(data[[3]])] <- 0

(You can use iData() rather than spectra() if you prefer. They are the same.)

Trying to assign into iData(data[[3]])[] will not work in your example, because you are returning an in-memory matrix, but not assigning it to a variable, so no data ends up changing. You need to assign the in-memory matrix back into the imaging data slot to be able to modify it this way.

If you do not want to load the data into memory and don't mind modifying the original on-disk data (presumably an imzML file), you can do:

readonly(spectra(data[[3]])) <- FALSE

for ( i in 1:ncol(data[[3]] )
    if ( anyNA(spectra(data[[3]][,i])
        spectra(data[[3]])[is.na(spectra(data[[3]][,i]),i] <- 0

(The next version of matter will support linear indexing so you will no longer need a 'for' loop, but a 'for' loop may be more efficient in this case anyway, depending on the size of the data.)

-Kylie

Edit: I will also change the normalize method to work with missing values in the next version. Missing values in spectra tends to break a lot of other things which is why it hasn't come up before.
